findings.summary: Every page's content is offset roughly half a page from its title, so each page opens with the previous chapter's material and closes with the next chapter's.
findings.evidence: Page 4 ("Quoting, Expansion, Word Splitting") opens with "Normal Non-Zero Exits" and the `-e` takeaway "`-e` is a safety net with holes"; page 5 ("ShellCheck: Your Static Analyzer") opens with "String Ops, No Subprocess" (`${p#*/}`, `${s,,}`); page 6 ("Temp Files Without Tears") opens with "Suppression, Done Right" and `.shellcheckrc`; page 8 ("Traps, Cleanup, and Signals") closes with "The Definition" — "Running N times leaves the same state as running once" — plus the idempotent-pairs table; page 9 ("Idempotency") closes with "Destroyers" (`rm -rf "$dir/"`, `cd "$dir" || exit 1`).
findings.fix: Re-cut the slide boundaries so each page holds only its titled chapter: move the trailing block run of each page onto the following page and the leading block run back onto the preceding one, then re-split into eleven pages matching the syllabus's ten chapters plus the extra "Atomic Writes, Locks, and Trap Basics" page.

findings.summary: The handbook's final chapter never arrives: page 10 ends with an accent heading and no content beneath it, and the entire "Production Script Checklist" chapter is absent.
findings.evidence: Page 10's last block is `{"type":"heading","text":"Skeleton, Top To Bottom","ink":"accent"}` with no block after it, while the caption promises "the full walk from `set -euo pipefail` to a shipping checklist" and the syllabus's chapter 10 covers `main "$@"`, `SCRIPT_DIR`, `die()`, exit codes, and secret handling — none of which appear anywhere in the deck.
findings.fix: Add an eleventh page titled "Production Script Checklist" carrying chapter 10's material (skeleton order, `main "$@"`, `SCRIPT_DIR=$(cd -- "$(dirname -- "${BASH_SOURCE[0]}")" && pwd)`, `die()`, exit codes 0/1/2, secrets-not-in-argv, the five-line safety core) and move the orphan "Skeleton, Top To Bottom" heading onto it as that page's opening heading.

findings.summary: Page 1 closes by describing a header line it never names, leaving the learner with instructions for an unidentified thing.
findings.evidence: The final bullets read "One line, top of file, after shebang / Before any logic, any sourcing, any variable / Four changes: silence becomes loud failure" — `set -euo pipefail` and `IFS=$'\n\t'` are not shown until page 2's "The Canonical Header".
findings.fix: Move this bullets block to page 2, immediately after the `set -euo pipefail` / `IFS=$'\n\t'` code block, so "four changes" refers to something already on screen.

findings.summary: The strict-mode page opens with a rule that depends on both strict mode and ShellCheck, neither of which has been shown yet.
findings.evidence: Page 2's first content block is "Touches files, credentials, prod? strict mode + shellcheck first" — "strict mode" is only defined later on the same page, and ShellCheck is not introduced until page 5.
findings.fix: Move the "Rules Of Thumb" heading and bullets back to page 1 (they are chapter 1 material), and replace "shellcheck" there with "a static analyzer (page 5)" so the forward reference is signposted rather than assumed.

findings.summary: The default-value expansion table states the `:+` and `:?` colon forms incorrectly — both key on "unset or empty", not on set/unset.
findings.evidence: Rows: ["`${v:?msg}`","unset: die with msg"] and ["`${v:+alt}`","only when SET"]. Bash manual: for `${parameter:+word}` "if parameter is null or unset, nothing is substituted"; `${parameter:?word}` errors "if parameter is null or unset". So `v=""` makes `${v:+alt}` expand to nothing (not "SET") and makes `${v:?msg}` die.
findings.fix: Change to ["`${v:+alt}`","set and non-empty"] and ["`${v:?msg}`","unset or empty: die"], matching the `:-`/`-` distinction the table's first two rows already draw.

findings.summary: The quoting page's closing bullets use ShellCheck flags and directives one page before ShellCheck is introduced.
findings.evidence: Page 4's final block reads "Without `-x`, sourced definitions look undefined / Gate CI at `warning`, tighten to `style` later / Fragment with no shebang: `# shellcheck shell=bash`" — but "Static analyzer for shell scripts" and "Four severities: error, warning, info, style" do not appear until page 5.
findings.fix: Move this bullets block onto page 5, placing it after the "Useful Flags" table where `-x`, `--severity=warning`, and `-s bash` have already been defined.

findings.summary: Page 4 is titled "Quoting, Expansion, Word Splitting" but its first three blocks close out page 3's `set -e` topic, and its last block jumps to ShellCheck.
findings.evidence: Page 4 opens with "Normal Non-Zero Exits" (`grep` "no match", `diff` "files differ"), bullets "Under `-e` an empty grep kills the script" / "Before 4.4 `$( )` does not inherit errexit", and the takeaway "`-e` is a safety net with holes" before "Rule One" starts the quoting material; it ends on "Without `-x`, sourced definitions look undefined" / "Gate CI at `warning`" / "`# shellcheck shell=bash`".
findings.fix: Move the exit-status table, the `-e` bullets and the "Bottom line" takeaway to page 3 ("Where set -e Lies To You") and the three ShellCheck bullets to page 5, so page 4 runs from "Rule One" to the `${var:?}` tip.

findings.summary: An unlabelled symlink-attack diagram closes the ShellCheck page, one page before the attack it depicts is explained.
findings.evidence: Page 5 ends with `{"type":"diagram","kind":"flow","spec":{"nodes":["attacker symlinks","script opens","writes as root","/etc/passwd owned"]}}`, while the explanation "Attacker pre-creates it as a symlink to `/etc/passwd` / Your script, running as root, writes through it" is on page 6.
findings.fix: Move the diagram to page 6, directly beneath the "Never Hardcode A Path" bullets that describe the attack.

findings.summary: Page 5 is titled "ShellCheck: Your Static Analyzer" but opens with parameter-expansion string surgery that has nothing to do with ShellCheck.
findings.evidence: The first two blocks are the code "${p#*/}  ${p##*/}   # trim prefix: short, long" / "${s/old/new} ${s//old/new}" and bullets "Kills `basename`, `dirname`, `sed`, `tr` subprocesses" / "Never put untrusted input in `$(( ))`"; ShellCheck is only introduced at the third block, "What It Is" — "Static analyzer for shell scripts".
findings.fix: Move the string-ops code block and its bullets onto page 4 ("Quoting, Expansion, Word Splitting"), where parameter expansion is already the subject, and let page 5 open on the "What It Is" heading.

findings.summary: Page 6 is titled "Temp Files Without Tears" but its first four blocks are ShellCheck suppression and linting-toolchain material that belongs to page 5.
findings.evidence: Page 6 opens with the code block "# shellcheck disable=SC2086 # splitting intended" / "# .shellcheckrc:" / "# severity=warning", then the heading "The Toolchain" with the flow "shfmt → shellcheck → bats-core → CI gate" and bullets "`shfmt -i 2 -ci -d` for formatting consistency" / "shellcheck = correctness, shfmt = style" — temp files only start at "Never Hardcode A Path".
findings.fix: Move the suppression code block, the "The Toolchain" heading, its flow diagram and its four bullets back onto page 5 ("ShellCheck: Your Static Analyzer"), so page 6 opens on "Never Hardcode A Path" and matches its title.

findings.summary: The idempotency table inverts the `cp` pair: plain `cp a b` is already idempotent by the deck's own definition, while `cp -n a b` is the one that fails to converge.
findings.evidence: Table row: ["`cp a b`","`cp -n a b`"] under headers ["Not idempotent","Idempotent"], against the definition given two blocks earlier: "Running N times leaves the same state as running once". Running `cp a b` twice leaves b identical to a both times; `cp -n a b` (bullet: "`cp -n` refuses to overwrite an existing target") leaves a stale pre-existing b in place forever, so run N and run 1 differ from the intended state.
findings.fix: Drop the `cp` row, or replace it with a genuinely non-idempotent/idempotent pair such as ["`cat a >> b`","`cp a b`"] / ["`tar -x` into a live dir","`rsync -a --delete a/ b/`"]. If `cp -n` is kept anywhere, label it "non-clobbering, NOT convergent".

findings.summary: Page 8 is titled "Traps, Cleanup, and Signals" but roughly its final third teaches idempotency, which is page 9's title.
findings.evidence: After "Signals And Children" the page continues with the heading "The Definition" ("Running N times leaves the same state as running once", "The property that makes retries safe"), the tip "Declare state, not steps", and the heading "Idempotent Pairs" with the `mkdir dir`/`mkdir -p dir`, `rm file`/`rm -f file` table — while page 9 is titled "Idempotency: Safe To Run Twice".
findings.fix: Shift the "The Definition", "Declare state, not steps" and "Idempotent Pairs" blocks onto page 9 so page 8 ends on the "Orphans are your fault" takeaway, and page 9 opens with the definition its title promises.

findings.summary: The section heading "Skeleton, Top To Bottom" renders with no body content beneath it, leaving an empty section and a large blank gap in the right column.
findings.evidence: Right column: "→ Skeleton, Top To Bottom" appears at roughly y=467, and the next content on the page is the separate full-width heading "→ Comparison Table" at roughly y=622 — nothing renders between them.
findings.fix: Either restore the missing bullets/code for the "Skeleton, Top To Bottom" block in the page source, or drop the heading so no empty section is emitted.

findings.summary: The caption claims the `cd`/`rm` disaster produces no error output, contradicting the deck's own slide showing `cd` writing to stderr.
findings.evidence: Caption: "`cd /nonexistent; rm -rf *` — two commands, one deleted working directory, zero error messages." Page 1 code comment: "cd /nonexistent   # fails, prints to stderr". `cd` prints "No such file or directory" and returns 1.
findings.fix: Change "zero error messages" to "one ignored error message" — the point is that the error is printed and then ignored, which is also the stronger framing.

findings.summary: The shebang table claims `#!/bin/sh` breaks `local`, but dash — the very shell the row names — implements `local`.
findings.evidence: Table row: ["`#!/bin/sh`","dash on Debian","arrays, `[[ ]]`, `local`"]. dash provides `local` as a (non-POSIX) builtin; it is documented in dash(1) and is why Debian policy scripts can use it.
findings.fix: Replace `local` in the Breaks cell with something dash genuinely lacks, e.g. "arrays, `[[ ]]`, `+=`, `${v^^}`, process substitution".

findings.summary: Says cron supplies "no PATH", when cron does set a PATH — just a minimal one — which is a different failure mode.
findings.evidence: Bullet: "cron: no PATH, no TTY, no profile sourced". Vixie/ISC cron sets `PATH=/usr/bin:/bin` and `SHELL=/bin/sh` for every job unless overridden in the crontab.
findings.fix: Change to "cron: PATH is `/usr/bin:/bin` only, no TTY, no profile sourced" — the point is that `~/.local/bin`, `/usr/local/bin` and friends are missing, not that PATH is unset.

findings.summary: "no arrays of data, only words" is wrong for bash and contradicts the deck's own array quoting guidance.
findings.evidence: Bullet: "Everything is text — no arrays of data, only words", while page 4 teaches "`\"$var\"` `\"$@\"` `\"$(cmd)\"` `\"${arr[@]}\"`". Bash has had indexed arrays since 2.0 and associative arrays since 4.0.
findings.fix: Reword to "Everything is text — flat indexed/associative arrays only, no nested data", which is both true and the actual reason the "Switch to Python: nested data structures" card exists.

findings.summary: Asserts Docker's `sh` is dash, but the most common minimal base image (Alpine) uses BusyBox ash.
findings.evidence: Bullet: "Docker: `sh` is dash, not bash". In Alpine images `/bin/sh` is a symlink to BusyBox ash; dash is only `sh` on Debian/Ubuntu-derived images.
findings.fix: Reword to "Docker: `sh` is dash (Debian) or BusyBox ash (Alpine) — never bash".

findings.summary: Presents `pipefail` on `grep x f | head` as pure upside, omitting that this exact pipeline is the canonical pipefail false-positive via SIGPIPE.
findings.evidence: Bullet: "`pipefail`: `grep x f | head` stops hiding grep", reusing page 1's example "grep x file | head  # grep failure hidden". When grep matches more than head consumes, head exits first, grep dies on SIGPIPE with status 141, and pipefail makes the successful pipeline return 141 — killing the script under `set -e`.
findings.fix: Add a caveat bullet: "pipefail + early-exiting readers (`head`, `grep -q`) turns SIGPIPE into exit 141 — wrap those pipelines with `|| [[ $? == 141 ]]` or restructure."

findings.summary: The `set -E` tip is justified entirely by ERR traps, a concept not introduced until five pages later.
findings.evidence: Page 2's callout reads "errtrace makes ERR traps fire inside functions, subshells and command substitutions. Without it your handler is decorative" — "`ERR` fires on failure under errexit — reporting hook" is on page 7.
findings.fix: Extend the callout with a half-sentence defining the term in place, e.g. "an ERR trap is a handler the shell runs when a command fails (page 7)", so "your handler" has a referent.

findings.summary: An unlabelled expansion-pipeline diagram ends the errexit page with no surrounding text tying it to anything on that page.
findings.evidence: Page 3's last block is `{"type":"diagram","kind":"flow","spec":{"nodes":["$var","IFS split","glob expand","argv"]}}`, following "Assignment Masking" code about `local x=$(failing_cmd)`; word splitting and globbing are page 4's subject.
findings.fix: Move the diagram to page 4 under "Rule One", next to the bullet "Unquoted `$var`: split on IFS, then glob-expanded", which is the caption it needs.

findings.summary: Recommends a `mktemp -t` template that the same page's portability table flags as GNU/BSD-divergent.
findings.evidence: Bullet: "Template: `mktemp -t myscript.XXXXXX`, X's required", followed by the table row ["`mktemp -t x.XXX`","GNU/BSD differ"] and ["`mktemp \"${TMPDIR:-/tmp}/x.XXXXXX\"`","portable"]. With BSD/macOS mktemp, `-t` takes a prefix and appends its own suffix; with GNU it takes a deprecated template.
findings.fix: Change the bullet to recommend the form the table calls portable: "Template: `mktemp \"${TMPDIR:-/tmp}/myscript.XXXXXX\"` — at least 3 X's, avoid `-t`."

findings.summary: The mktemp pattern hands the learner a `trap` line as a mandatory step before traps, pseudo-signals, or `EXIT` have been explained.
findings.evidence: Page 6 shows `trap 'rm -rf -- "${tmpdir:?}"' EXIT  # next line!` and asserts "Pair with cleanup on the VERY next line", but "`trap 'handler' SIGNAL` registers code for a signal" and "`EXIT` fires on every exit path" first appear on page 7.
findings.fix: Add a one-line gloss beside the code — e.g. "`trap … EXIT` runs the command on every exit path; full mechanics next page" — so the pattern is copy-pasteable without a forward jump.

findings.summary: States that the ERR trap fires "under errexit", implying `set -e` is a prerequisite, which it is not.
findings.evidence: Bullet: "`ERR` fires on failure under errexit — reporting hook". Bash fires the ERR trap whenever a simple command/pipeline returns non-zero subject to the errexit exemption list, independently of whether `set -e` is enabled — which is why an ERR trap is usable as a pure reporting hook in non-strict scripts.
findings.fix: Reword to "`ERR` fires on any unguarded non-zero command — same exemptions as `-e`, but works without it".

findings.summary: The title "Atomic Writes, Locks, and Trap Basics" splits traps across two consecutively titled pages while omitting the temp-file-avoidance material the page actually opens with.
findings.evidence: Page 7 opens with "Skip The File Entirely" (`diff <(sort a) <(sort b)`, heredocs, `cmd <<< "$var"`) and the "Secrets: pipe, not path" callout — neither atomic writes nor locks nor traps — while "Trap Basics" in the title duplicates page 8's "Traps, Cleanup, and Signals".
findings.fix: Retitle page 7 "Atomic Writes, Locks, and Umask" and drop "Trap Basics" (moving "The Shell's Finally Block", the signal table and "Quote At Registration" to page 8), or retitle it to name the process-substitution content, e.g. "Skip The File: Pipes, Atomic Writes, Locks".

findings.summary: The Destroyers block claims an empty `$dir` turns `rm -rf "$dir/"` into a working `rm -rf /`, but GNU rm has refused to recurse on `/` by default since coreutils 6.4.
findings.evidence: Code: "rm -rf \"$dir/\"      # $dir empty = rm -rf /". GNU coreutils manual, "Treating / specially": `--preserve-root` is the default and rm "declines to operate on any directory that resolves to /" unless `--no-preserve-root` is given (BSD/macOS rm likewise refuses "/"). The expansion here is the single argument `/`, which is refused.
findings.fix: Use the hazard that actually still fires: `rm -rf "$dir"/*` (empty `$dir` ⇒ `rm -rf /*`, which preserve-root does NOT block), and keep `${dir:?}` as the fix — that is also ShellCheck SC2115's own example.

findings.summary: Page 10, titled "Footgun Gallery", ends with a section heading its title does not cover and which has no content beneath it.
findings.evidence: The final block of page 10 is the heading "Skeleton, Top To Bottom" (ink "accent") with no bullets, code or table after it; the checklist it announces only appears in Part 2 ("Production Script Checklist", "The Five-Line Core").
findings.fix: Delete the dangling "Skeleton, Top To Bottom" heading from page 10 so the page ends on the redirection code block, and let Part 2's "Production Script Checklist" carry that section.
